tip: καλύτερα (kalítera) with -a is 'better' as an adverb: νιώθω καλύτερα (niótho kalítera) = I feel better. The -ος form describes nouns; the -α form describes the verb.
'Worse' is one word: χειρότερη (chiróteri), the irregular partner of καλύτερος (kalíteros). No 'more' needed: χειρότερη από ποτέ (chiróteri apó poté) = worse than ever.
μεγαλύτερος (megalíteros) means both bigger AND older – context decides. Here μεγαλύτερη από εμένα (megalíteri apó eména) = older than me, not physically bigger.
Shoe size is νούμερο (número); clothing size is μέγεθος (mégethos). So in a shoe shop: σε μεγαλύτερο νούμερο (se megalítero número) = in a bigger size.
μικρότερος (mikróteros) covers both smaller AND younger: ο μικρότερος γιος (o mikróteros yos) = the youngest son, not the smallest one.
το χειρότερο (to chirótero) = the worst thing – το + adjective alone works as a noun, no 'thing' needed. Same trick: το καλύτερο (to kalítero) = the best part.
πιο πολλά (pio pollá) = more, in the plural – because the unspoken word is τα λεφτά (ta leftá) = money, which is itself plural in Greek.
καφέ (kafé) = brown, borrowed from 'coffee' – and loanword colors never change form: τα καφέ παπούτσια (ta kafé papútsia), same καφέ (kafé) for any gender or number.
δεν μου πάει (den mu pái) is literally 'it doesn't go to me' = it doesn't suit me. Colors and clothes 'go to' people in Greek.
κρατάει (kratái) is 'holds' – and a thing that holds, lasts: κρατάει χρόνια (kratái chrónia) = it lasts for years.
φοράτε (foráte) is the polite plural – shop staff use it with any single customer: τι μέγεθος φοράτε; (ti mégethos foráte) = what size do you wear?
χτυπάω (chtipáo) is 'hit' – tight shoes literally hit you in Greek: με χτυπάνε (me chtipáne) = they pinch me.
δεν μου κάνει (den mu káni) is literally 'it doesn't do for me' = it doesn't fit me. For sizes and gear, things 'do' for you in Greek.
Brown splits in Greek: καστανά (kastaná) for eyes and hair, καφέ (kafé) for objects like shoes – swap them and it sounds off.
έχει ζωή (échi zoí) is literally 'it has life' = it's lively. Greek places 'have' their qualities: έχει κόσμο (échi kósmo) = it's crowded.
τόσο... όσο (tóso... óso) = as... as: τόσο ακριβό όσο φαίνεται (tóso akrivó óso fénete) = as expensive as it seems.
με πρωινό (me proinó) = with breakfast, no article – Greek drops 'the' when asking what's included. Same with με θέα (me théa) = with a view.
One-off commands use the short past stem: κλείσε (klíse) = book!, from κλείνω (klíno). The -ν- becomes -σ- because you mean do it once, not keep doing it.
μου (mu) has no accent of its own, so στο όνομά μου (sto ónomá mu) grows a second accent – without it, the stress would sit too far from the end of the word chain.
καλή διαμονή (kalí diamoní) = enjoy your stay – καλή/καλό + noun is the all-purpose Greek wish: καλό ταξίδι (kaló taxídi) = safe trip.
υπάρχει (ipárchi) = there is – a notch more formal than plain έχει (échi). Both work at the desk: υπάρχει πάρκινγκ; or έχει πάρκινγκ; (échi párking).
Apologizing is literally asking: μας ζήτησαν συγγνώμη (mas zítisan signómi) = 'they asked us forgiveness'. The person wronged appears as a plain object pronoun – μας (mas).
Two past tenses, two jobs: φυσούσε (fisúse) = the wind was blowing, an ongoing scene; άργησε (árgise) = it was late, one finished event.
περιμέναμε (periméname) is imperfect: the waiting stretched on with no single endpoint. Almost three hours calls for the tense that paints duration.
είχε κύμα (íche kíma) is literally 'it had wave' = the sea was rough. The sea 'has' its conditions in Greek – no adjective needed.
έδεσε (édese) is literally 'it tied' – ships dock by tying up, so Greek just says the boat tied: το πλοίο έδεσε (to plío édese).
Greek stacks negatives: δεν έφυγε κανένα πλοίο (den éfiye kanéna plío) = no boat left. κανένα (kanéna) and δεν (den) are both required – not an error.
ταξιδεύαμε (taxidévame) is imperfect, the all-night background; φτάσαμε (ftásame) is aorist, the arrival that caps it. Scene in one tense, event in the other.
η θάλασσα ήταν λάδι (i thálassa ítan ládi) is literally 'the sea was oil' – Greek's standard image for a dead-calm, glassy sea.
γυρίζω (yirízo) means both go around AND come back – context decides. Here γυρίσαμε όλο το νησί (yirísame ólo to nisí) = we went around the whole island.
δίπλα στο κύμα (dípla sto kíma) is literally 'next to the wave' – the standard Greek way to say a place sits right on the water.
δεν θέλαμε (den thélame) is imperfect because wanting is a state, not an event – the not-wanting-to-leave lasted the whole end of the trip.
τους δύο (tus dío) with the article means 'the two' = both. Bare δύο (dío) just counts; και για τους δύο (ke ya tus dío) = for both of them.
Both verbs are imperfect – ήταν (ítan) and οδηγούσαμε (odigúsame) – pure scene-setting: the road stayed dirt, the driving stayed slow, nothing 'happens' yet.
μένω από (méno apó) is literally 'be left from' = to run out of: έμεινε από βενζίνη (émine apó venzíni) = it ran out of petrol.
Commands negate with μη(ν) (min), not δεν (den): μην οδηγείς (min odiyís) = don't ride. δεν (den) states facts; μη(ν) (min) forbids.
ένα βράδυ (éna vrádi) + aorist pins one specific evening, one finished event: φάγαμε (fágame) = we ate, that night and done.
ξαφνικά (xafniká) = suddenly pairs with the aorist: νύχτωσε (níchtose) = night fell, one sharp event. Sudden things take the one-shot past tense.
The classic pair: imperfect περπατούσαμε (perpatúsame) = we were walking, the backdrop; aorist είδαμε (ídame) = we saw, the event that cuts in.
έλεγε (éleye) is imperfect for a habit: grandma told stories evening after evening. One single telling would be είπε (ípe).
γνωρίζω (gnorízo) = to know, but its one-shot past means met for the first time: γνωρίσαμε (gnorísame) = we met. The knowing began at one moment.
με πήρε ο ύπνος (me píre o ípnos) is literally 'sleep took me' = I dozed off. Sleep is the doer in Greek; you're just the one it grabs.
χορεύαμε (chorévame) is imperfect even with ένα βράδυ (éna vrádi) – the point is that the dancing went on for hours, and duration beats the one-night frame.
αξίζει να (axízi na) + verb = it's worth ...ing: αξίζει να πας (axízi na pas) = it's worth going – no 'it' subject needed.
έχει κόσμο (échi kósmo) is literally 'it has people' = it's crowded. Impersonal έχει covers conditions too: έχει ζέστη (échi zésti) = it's hot.
